## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
\begin{marginfigure}
\resizebox{0.92\linewidth}{!}{\mlphysicalstackfull{20}{20}{20}{20}{20}}
\caption{The five-level machine stack within the governance envelope.}
\end{marginfigure}
:::

_Under what auditable chain of physical evidence is an autonomous machine permitted to move among humans?_

Releasing an autonomous machine grants software the authority to exert physical forces in unconstrained environments alongside human beings. That deployment authority demands an auditable safety case connecting operational claims directly to empirical evidence from the integrated physical plant. High validation accuracy cannot guarantee that a robot stops within available clearance envelopes, nor can an incident-free test log confirm that emergency fallbacks remain dependable when critical sensors experience silent hardware faults.

A release decision must identify precisely which empirical measurements support each warrant and explicitly delineate the environmental assumptions bounding their validity. Unmodeled payload shifts, floor wear, or thermal drift can instantly invalidate a safety case even when neural weights remain unaltered; where evidence cannot settle an operating premise, refusal is the only acceptable engineering verdict. Within the governance envelope, deployment release consolidates the Brain's proposals, the Nervous System's permission path, and the Body's physical limits into an auditable manifest that revokes motion authority the instant evidence expires.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Construct a claim-argument-evidence case linking a bounded operating envelope to auditable physical evidence
- Evaluate whether each claim's premises are measured, illustrative, or unknown, and select the verdict they support
- Identify the measurements that would lift a refusal and the restrictions a conditional verdict would keep
- Specify standing conditions that withdraw operating authority when wear, drift, or configuration changes invalidate a release
- Diagnose unsupported warrants and compound defeaters through adversarial review of a release argument
- Design a release manifest that binds its upstream records by digest and refuses motion on any mismatch

:::

## The Decision to Deploy {#sec-release-decision-to-deploy}

A directory of passing test records and hardware fault traces does not by itself decide whether an autonomous machine may move among people. In a web service, a regression in a new build costs a rollback and some corrupted records. In physical AI, release delegates authority over mass, force, and velocity. Verification has already stressed the machine's timing, contention, and sensing assumptions under injected faults, and what it hands over is its fault records, each with a predeclared oracle, and the gaps they leave. The engineering task therefore shifts from finding defects to bounding what the evidence licenses. Neither validation accuracy (@sec-evaluation-closed-loop-dynamics) nor a run of clean demonstrations (@sec-verification-fault-injection) meets that task, and deciding to deploy is not a statistical prediction. It is an engineering adjudication of whether the evidence bounds the physical risk of operation in a named domain.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↰ **Prerequisite:** The empirical verification evidence backing release claims is produced in @sec-verification-hardware-fault-injection.
:::

The release this chapter works through is the warehouse mobile manipulator's service at one site: driving the aisles past rack ends where a person may be standing, opening the spring-latched cage door, and handing the ceramic mug it takes from the takeaway conveyor to the coworker at the packing station. Each job carries its own criterion, a clear distance for the base and a contact force for the arm, and model accuracy establishes none of them. Release therefore depends on pre-contact clearance, measured brake capability, a bounded full response path, and the signed fault records of @sec-verification-fault-manifest.

A release verdict is a bounded, revocable judgment. The chapter builds that judgment from the operating envelope, a claim-argument-evidence tree, three signed verdicts, the standing conditions whose failure revokes a verdict, a worked adjudication and the adversarial review it must survive, and a release manifest that refuses motion when the running machine no longer matches its signed evidence.

## The Release Question {#sec-release-question}

For the mobile manipulator, the release question is whether the evidence meets the physical criterion of each of its three jobs inside a scoped envelope. The argument names the physical bounds, specified fault set, and validated permission and fallback path. It can support a revocable grant of tracking authority while those conditions hold; it cannot infer protection against every possible fault from finite tests (\ref{dfn-release-goal-structured-safety-case}).

::: {#dfn-release-goal-structured-safety-case .callout-definition title="Claim-argument-evidence safety case"}

***Claim-argument-evidence safety case***\index{Claim-argument-evidence safety case!definition}\index{Safety case!physical AI} is the auditable, structured assurance argument for a specified physical machine, operating envelope, hazard criteria, and fault model, linking top-level safety claims to concrete empirical evidence through explicit engineering warrants.

1.  **Significance**: Transforms subjective, informal deployment confidence into an auditable, falsifiable engineering argument that connects high-level safety goals to concrete empirical evidence across the entire physical stack.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike software unit test suites or static model validation scorecards, a physical safety case explicitly links operational design domain boundaries, hardware fault injection logs, and runtime enforcer tripwires to demonstrate bounded residual risk.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Treating the safety case as a retrospective compliance checklist completed after development, rather than a living architectural contract that governs feature integration and release gating.

:::

```{python}
#| label: calc-release-operating-envelope
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE MACHINE'S OPERATING ENVELOPE FOR RELEASE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-release-question (envelope and conditional-zone paragraphs),
# │          @tbl-16-odd-invariants, the contact-criteria paragraph after it, and
# │          the binding-contract paragraphs of @sec-release-three-verdicts, and
# │          the empirical-sufficiency probe of @sec-release-adversarial-review.
# │ Goal: Scope the release case to the running machine's operating envelope.
# │ Show: aisle speed and its ceiling, tote-rack payload, the friction bands and
# │       the inspected-floor ceiling, the clear distance, the latch and handover
# │       speeds with their limits, the slow-downs before a takeover, and the
# │       restricted speed on inspected floors.
# │ How: RM/AISLE fields; ceilings from calc_max_permitted_velocity with a_eff,
# │      the constant deceleration whose distance matches calc_c2_stop_suffix,
# │      and the three overheads; mu_min = a_brake/g.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_velocity, fmt_length, fmt_mass, fmt_force, fmt_latency, check
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_max_permitted_velocity, calc_c2_effective_deceleration

# ┌── 1. LOAD: the running machine and its site ─────────────────────────────────
RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator  # category: illustrative (running machine)
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle  # category: illustrative (aisle scene; speeds, lease, and tick chosen)
g_std = (1 * ureg.standard_gravity).to(meter / second**2)  # category: datasheet (standard gravity, a defined physical constant; Pint)
v_restricted = 1.0 * meter / second  # category: chosen (scenario assumption: restricted mode on inspected floors, the value @sec-frontier uses)

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE: ceilings and friction bands ───────────────────────────────────
a_eff = calc_c2_effective_deceleration(AISLE.a_brake)  # C2 stop suffix as an equivalent constant deceleration
overhead_loc = AISLE.delta_loc + AISLE.eps_track
v_ceiling = calc_max_permitted_velocity(AISLE.d_clear, AISLE.tau_delay, a_eff, overhead_loc, AISLE.delta_margin).to(meter / second)
mu_min = (AISLE.a_brake / g_std).to("dimensionless").magnitude
a_inspected = min(AISLE.a_brake, (AISLE.mu_inspected_floor * g_std).to(meter / second**2))
v_inspected_ceiling = calc_max_permitted_velocity(
    AISLE.d_clear, AISLE.tau_delay, calc_c2_effective_deceleration(a_inspected), overhead_loc, AISLE.delta_margin
).to(meter / second)
v_handover_ceiling = (AISLE.f_contact_criterion / (AISLE.k_contact_human * RM.arm_effective_contact_mass) ** 0.5).to(meter / second)

# ┌── 3. GUARD: canon values quoted in the prose and the table ──────────────────
check(abs(v_ceiling.magnitude - 1.3898) < 5e-5, "Unconditional aisle speed ceiling is 1.39 m/s")
check(AISLE.v_aisle < v_ceiling, "Chosen aisle speed sits under its ceiling")
check(abs(mu_min - 0.204) < 5e-4, "Friction floor is 0.204")
check(mu_min < AISLE.mu_dry, "Dry concrete exceeds the friction floor")
check(mu_min > AISLE.mu_inspected_floor, "Inspected floor requires speed restriction")
check(abs(v_inspected_ceiling.magnitude - 1.0947) < 5e-5, "Restricted ceiling on inspected floors is 1.09 m/s")
check(v_restricted < v_inspected_ceiling, "Chosen restricted mode sits under its ceiling")
check(abs(v_handover_ceiling.magnitude - 0.1179) < 5e-5, "Coworker handover speed ceiling is 0.118 m/s")
check(AISLE.v_handover < v_handover_ceiling, "Chosen handover speed sits under its ceiling")
check(abs(RM.loaded_mass.to(kilogram).magnitude - 368.0) < 1e-9, "Running-machine loaded mass is 368 kg")
check(AISLE.v_takeover_in_loop < AISLE.v_aisle, "Slow-down before an in-loop takeover")
check(AISLE.mu_oil_film < AISLE.mu_inspected_floor < mu_min < AISLE.mu_dry, "Friction bands are ordered")
check(abs(AISLE.v_aisle.to(meter / second).magnitude - 1.3) < 1e-9, "Signed aisle speed 1.3 m/s")
check(abs(AISLE.d_clear.to(meter).magnitude - 1.10) < 1e-9, "Clear distance 1.10 m")
check(abs(AISLE.v_takeover_in_loop.to(meter / second).magnitude - 1.2) < 1e-9, "In-loop takeover slow-down 1.2 m/s")
check(abs(AISLE.v_takeover_out_of_loop.to(meter / second).magnitude - 0.3) < 1e-9, "Out-of-loop takeover slow-down 0.3 m/s")
check(abs(AISLE.t_tick.to(millisecond).magnitude - 1.0) < 1e-9, "Permission tick 1 ms")
check(AISLE.t_tick < AISLE.t_lease, "Servo tick sits inside the chunk lease")
check(abs(RM.onboard_payload_capacity.to(kilogram).magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, "Tote-rack capacity is 50 kg")
check(
    abs(AISLE.mu_dry - 0.60) < 1e-9 and abs(AISLE.mu_inspected_floor - 0.12) < 1e-9 and abs(AISLE.mu_oil_film - 0.05) < 1e-9,
    "Friction bands 0.60, 0.12, 0.05",
)
check(abs(AISLE.v_latch_approach.to(meter / second).magnitude - 0.03) < 1e-9, "Guarded latch approach 0.03 m/s")
check(abs(AISLE.v_latch_high.to(meter / second).magnitude - 0.10) < 1e-9, "Unsupported latch approach 0.10 m/s")
check(abs(AISLE.f_latch_tripwire.to(newton).magnitude - 15.0) < 1e-9, "Latch tripwire 15 N")
check(abs(AISLE.t_contact_response.to(millisecond).magnitude - 2.0) < 1e-9, "Contact-loop response 2 ms")
check(abs(AISLE.f_latch_limit.to(newton).magnitude - 100.0) < 1e-9, "Latch limit 100 N")
check(abs(AISLE.v_handover.to(meter / second).magnitude - 0.10) < 1e-9, "Handover speed 0.10 m/s")
check(abs(AISLE.f_contact_criterion.to(newton).magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, "Handover criterion 50 N")

# ┌── 4. OUTPUT: rendered values ────────────────────────────────────────────────
class ReleaseEnvelope:
    v_restricted = v_restricted  # chosen; read by calc-release-worked-verdict
    v_aisle_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_aisle, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    v_ceiling_str = fmt_velocity(round(v_ceiling.magnitude, 2) * meter / second, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    v_takeover_in_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_takeover_in_loop, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    v_takeover_out_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_takeover_out_of_loop, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    t_tick_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.t_tick, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    payload_str = fmt_mass(RM.onboard_payload_capacity, unit=kilogram, precision=0)
    m1_str = fmt_mass(RM.loaded_mass, unit=kilogram, precision=0)
    mu_min_str = fmt(round(mu_min, 3), precision=3)
    mu_dry_str = fmt(AISLE.mu_dry, precision=2)
    mu_inspected_str = fmt(AISLE.mu_inspected_floor, precision=2)
    mu_oil_str = fmt(AISLE.mu_oil_film, precision=2)
    v_inspected_ceiling_str = fmt_velocity(round(v_inspected_ceiling.magnitude, 2) * meter / second, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    v_restricted_str = fmt_velocity(v_restricted, unit=meter / second, precision=0)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(AISLE.d_clear, unit=meter, precision=2)
    v_latch_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_latch_approach, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    v_latch_high_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_latch_high, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    f_trip_str = fmt_force(AISLE.f_latch_tripwire, precision=0)
    t_contact_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.t_contact_response, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    f_latch_limit_str = fmt_force(AISLE.f_latch_limit, precision=0)
    v_handover_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_handover, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    v_handover_ceiling_str = fmt_velocity(round(v_handover_ceiling.magnitude, 3) * meter / second, unit=meter / second, precision=3)
    f_contact_str = fmt_force(AISLE.f_contact_criterion, precision=0)
```

A release case is scoped by the operating envelope, the target ODD paired with the machine's own internal conditions. An unconditional (`UNCOND`) verdict authorizes the whole operating envelope (@sec-verification-operating-envelope), a conditional (`COND`) verdict a named part of it, and a refusal (`REFUSE`) none.\index{Operational design domain!release verdicts} For the mobile manipulator, the operating envelope admits aisle travel at up to `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_aisle_str` (chosen; see the Reader Guide) with the tote rack loaded to at most `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.payload_str`, on floors surveyed to a friction coefficient of at least `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.mu_min_str`, past rack ends with at least `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.d_clear_str` of clear distance. It admits door approaches at `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_latch_str` and item handovers to the coworker at `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_handover_str`.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↰ **Prerequisite:** The operational design domain and its known absences are defined in @sec-data-policy-coverage.
:::

Inside these boundaries the learned policy may propose actions across the nominal task envelope, but each action still requires independent permission. Conditional states of the monitored dimensions (@tbl-16-odd-invariants) narrow that envelope; for example, the machine slows to `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_takeover_in_str` before it requests an in-loop takeover. The restricted mode of a `COND` verdict narrows it further, so on a floor known only through the site's inspection regime the machine runs at `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_restricted_str`, below the `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_inspected_ceiling_str` inspected-floor ceiling.

As formalized in @tbl-16-odd-invariants, each monitored dimension is partitioned into nominal, conditional, and refusal states. A conditional state restricts admitted proposals. A refusal state withdraws tracking permission and selects a validated fallback (@sec-enforcement-fallback-ladder). The table lists the dimensions within which a runtime monitor or a site procedure keeps the machine; the internal conditions of @sec-verification-operating-envelope, such as ambient temperature, rail voltage, and compute load, enter through the fault records trialed at them.

\Needspace{28\baselineskip}

| Envelope Dimension / Invariant | Nominal Envelope ($\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{nom}}$)                                                                           | Conditional Boundary ($\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{cond}}$)                                                                                                                                                        | Hard Refusal ($\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{refuse}}$)                                                                                                                         | Runtime Monitor & Rate                                                                 | Enforcer Action & Latency                                                      |
|:-------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Aisle Speed**                | $v\le$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_aisle_str`                                                                             | `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_takeover_in_str` before an in-loop takeover request; `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_takeover_out_str` before an out-of-loop one                                                    | Measured speed above the signed `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_aisle_str` (ceiling `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_ceiling_str`), or invalid speed estimate                   | Encoders and IMU, every `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.t_tick_str` permission tick          | Clamp admitted speed; refuse above the signed speed                            |
| **Floor Friction**             | Surveyed $\mu\ge$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.mu_min_str` (dry concrete near `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.mu_dry_str`)         | Inspection regime only ($\mu\ge$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.mu_inspected_str`): restricted `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_restricted_str`, below the `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_inspected_ceiling_str` ceiling | Unsurveyed floor or reported film; a clear oil film ($\mu\approx$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.mu_oil_str`) is invisible to the cameras                                   | Floor survey and site spill procedure; no on-board measurement                         | Restrict speed by floor zone; refuse the aisle                                 |
| **Tote-Rack Payload**          | $0\le m\le$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.payload_str`, valid load estimate (total at most `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.m1_str`) | Estimate stale since the last pick: stationary arm tasks only                                                                                                                                               | Load above capacity or invalid estimate                                                                                                                                | Rack load cells, at each pick                                                          | Refuse aisle transit until re-weighed                                          |
| **Rack-End Clearance**         | Surveyed $D_{\text{clear}}\ge$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.d_clear_str` at every rack end                                   | Shorter surveyed clearance: lower signed speed from the same budget                                                                                                                                         | Unsurveyed rack end, or obstacle inside the clear distance                                                                                                             | Site survey; lidar and navigation camera at frame rate                                 | Speed limit per rack end; stop for a detected obstacle                         |
| **Door Latch Approach**        | $v\le$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_latch_str`, strike plate at its nominal position                                       | None; demonstrations cover no other latch condition                                                                                                                                                         | `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_latch_high_str` approach or displaced plate                                                                                                | Arm contact-force sensing in the `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.t_contact_str` contact loop | Trip at `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.f_trip_str`; refuse the unsupported approach |
| **Coworker Handover**          | TCP speed $\le$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_handover_str` under `accept_item`                                             | Coworker present without `accept_item`: hold short of the handover point                                                                                                                                    | TCP speed above the signed `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_handover_str` (ceiling `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_handover_ceiling_str`), or contact outside the assessed case | Joint encoders every permission tick; arm contact-force sensing                        | Clamp TCP speed; refuse above the signed speed                                 |

: **Operating envelope of the warehouse mobile manipulator**: Each listed dimension has disjoint nominal, conditional, and refusal intervals. Conditional operation requires every dimension to remain in a signed admissible interval; missing or invalid measurements refuse. Sensor rates and stopping response are plant validation obligations. {#tbl-16-odd-invariants tbl-colwidths="[16,16,18,18,16,16]"}

A defensible release claim states its plant, contact geometry, and fault set.[^fn-std-isots15066-biomech] The machine's case uses three criteria. The base stops inside the `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.d_clear_str` clear distance before it reaches a person who has stepped out at a rack end, the arm opens the door without exceeding the `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.f_latch_limit_str` latch limit, and a handover never presses on the coworker with more than a chosen `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.f_contact_str` peak force for an assessed contact case. The base's claim protects a stationary person; a person still walking toward the machine is a separate premise, carried by a site crossing rule (@sec-memory-belief-through-occlusion). The release argument must demonstrate which human contacts are excluded before impact, which detected contacts the model covers, and which single faults the independent fallback handles. A stop after contact does not by itself cap the first force peak.[^fn-math-contact-mechanics]

[^fn-std-isots15066-biomech]: **ISO/TS 15066 Biomechanical Limits**\index{ISO/TS 15066!biomechanical limits}: The specification gives body-region- and contact-type-dependent force and pressure data [@isots15066]. A site assessment must select the applicable body region, contact geometry, and measurement procedure. The handover criterion used here is a conservative case criterion, not a universal ISO/TS 15066 threshold or an injury boundary.

[^fn-math-contact-mechanics]: **Contact Mechanics Force Model**\index{Contact mechanics!force model}: The elastodynamic model couples translational kinetic energy, effective moving inertia, and contact interface stiffness to determine transient peak impact force during an unmitigated collision. Impacting a rigid boundary concentrates stored kinetic energy into a sub-millisecond impulse with severe force amplification, whereas elastic compliance extends deformation time and dissipates energy over a longer stroke. For the formal elastodynamic derivation and unilateral contact formulations, see @sec-appendix-control-contact.

```{python}
#| label: calc-release-biomechanical-impact-envelope
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ HANDOVER CONTACT FORCE AND THE BASE'S STOPPING SPARE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-release-question, @eq-release-unbraked-force and the two
# │          paragraphs after it (spare spent as delay), and the refusal
# │          paragraph of @sec-release-three-verdicts (the deceleration the
# │          budget assumes).
# │ Goal: Show why the arm's handover speed is capped, and how little input
# │       error the base's finished budget can absorb at aisle speed.
# │ Show: unbraked force at the free-space TCP limit and at the handover speed;
# │       budget and spare at 1.3 m/s; the delay and the deceleration shortfall
# │       that each consume the spare.
# │ How: calc_transient_impact_force with the arm's effective contact mass and
# │      the coworker tissue stiffness; calc_safe_stopping_distance with a_eff,
# │      the constant deceleration whose distance matches calc_c2_stop_suffix,
# │      and the three overheads.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import (
    fmt_mass,
    fmt_stiffness,
    fmt_force,
    fmt_multiple,
    fmt_latency,
    fmt_acceleration,
    fmt_length,
    fmt_velocity,
    fmt_percent,
    fmt_sci_qty,
    check,
)
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import (
    calc_safe_stopping_distance,
    calc_transient_impact_force,
    calc_c2_stop_suffix,
    calc_c2_effective_deceleration,
)

# ┌── 1. LOAD: the running machine and its site ─────────────────────────────────
RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator  # category: illustrative (running machine)
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle  # category: illustrative (aisle scene; speeds, lease, and tick chosen)

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE: contact forces, then the budget at aisle speed ────────────────
m_eff = RM.arm_effective_contact_mass
f_at_tcp_limit = calc_transient_impact_force(RM.tcp_speed_limit, m_eff, AISLE.k_contact_human).to(newton)
f_ratio = (f_at_tcp_limit / AISLE.f_contact_criterion).to("dimensionless").magnitude
f_at_handover = calc_transient_impact_force(AISLE.v_handover, m_eff, AISLE.k_contact_human).to(newton)
v_handover_ceiling = (AISLE.f_contact_criterion / (AISLE.k_contact_human * m_eff) ** 0.5).to(meter / second)

c2_braking = calc_c2_stop_suffix(AISLE.v_aisle, AISLE.a_brake)["distance"].to(meter)
a_eff = calc_c2_effective_deceleration(AISLE.a_brake)  # C2 stop suffix as an equivalent constant deceleration
overhead_loc = AISLE.delta_loc + AISLE.eps_track
budget_aisle = calc_safe_stopping_distance(AISLE.v_aisle, AISLE.tau_delay, a_eff, overhead_loc, AISLE.delta_margin).to(millimeter)
spare_aisle = (AISLE.d_clear - budget_aisle).to(millimeter)
t_spare = (spare_aisle / AISLE.v_aisle).to(millisecond)
# Deceleration at which the budget exactly fills the clear distance. The C2
# braking distance scales as 1/a, so a' = a_brake * d_C2(a_brake) / room.
braking_room = (AISLE.d_clear - AISLE.v_aisle * AISLE.tau_delay - overhead_loc - AISLE.delta_margin).to(meter)
a_break_even = (AISLE.a_brake * c2_braking / braking_room).to(meter / second**2)
a_shortfall_pct = ((AISLE.a_brake - a_break_even) / AISLE.a_brake).to("dimensionless").magnitude * 100.0

# ┌── 3. GUARD: canon values quoted in the prose ────────────────────────────────
check(abs(m_eff.to(kilogram).magnitude - 12.0) < 1e-9, "Effective contact mass is 12.0 kg")
check(abs(f_at_tcp_limit.magnitude - 424.26) < 0.01, "Unbraked force at the TCP limit")
check(abs(f_ratio - 8.49) < 0.01, "About 8.5x the 50 N criterion")
check(abs(f_at_handover.magnitude - 42.43) < 0.01, "Handover force is 42.4 N")
check(abs(v_handover_ceiling.magnitude - 0.1179) < 5e-5, "Handover ceiling is 0.118 m/s")
check(AISLE.v_handover < v_handover_ceiling, "Chosen handover speed sits under its ceiling")
check(abs(budget_aisle.magnitude - 997.43) < 5e-3, "Finished budget at 1.3 m/s")
check(abs(spare_aisle.magnitude - 102.57) < 5e-3, "Spare at 1.3 m/s")
check(abs(t_spare.magnitude - 78.9) < 0.05, "Spare spent as delay is 78.9 ms")
check(abs(a_shortfall_pct - 13.9) < 0.1, "A 14 percent deceleration shortfall fills the spare")

# ┌── 4. OUTPUT: rendered values ────────────────────────────────────────────────
class BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope:
    m_eff_str = fmt_mass(m_eff, unit=kilogram, precision=0)
    v_tcp_str = fmt_velocity(RM.tcp_speed_limit, unit=meter / second, precision=0)
    k_h_str = fmt_stiffness(AISLE.k_contact_human, unit=newton / meter, precision=0, commas=True)
    f_tcp_str = fmt_force(round(f_at_tcp_limit.magnitude) * newton, precision=0)
    f_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(f_ratio, precision=1)
    f_limit_str = fmt_force(AISLE.f_contact_criterion, precision=0)
    v_handover_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_handover, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    f_handover_str = fmt_force(f_at_handover, precision=1)
    v_handover_ceiling_str = fmt_velocity(round(v_handover_ceiling.magnitude, 3) * meter / second, unit=meter / second, precision=3)
    v_aisle_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_aisle, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(AISLE.d_clear, unit=meter, precision=2)
    budget_str = fmt_length(round(budget_aisle.magnitude, 1) * millimeter, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    spare_str = fmt_length(round(spare_aisle.magnitude, 1) * millimeter, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    t_spare_str = fmt_latency(round(t_spare.magnitude, 1) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    a_brake_str = fmt_acceleration(AISLE.a_brake, unit=meter / second**2, precision=0)
    a_shortfall_pct_str = fmt_percent(round(a_shortfall_pct) / 100.0, precision=0, style="prose")
```

Consider the arm at its free-space speed limit of `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.v_tcp_str`, with a robot-side effective mass at the tool center point of `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.m_eff_str`. In an unbraked elastic contact with the coworker's hand, modeled with an effective tissue stiffness $k_h$ of `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.k_h_str`, the peak contact force follows @eq-release-unbraked-force:
$$F_{\text{unbraked}} = v\,\sqrt{k_h\,m_{\text{eff}}}$$ {#eq-release-unbraked-force}
At the free-space limit this ideal elastic model predicts `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.f_tcp_str`, or `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.f_ratio_mult_str` the `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.f_limit_str` criterion, so the arm cannot enter an unseparated contact at that speed without a stronger, measured protection argument. The same equation bounds the item-handover speed that the enforcement record caps (@sec-enforcement-telemetry, @sec-intervention-human-authority), since the criterion admits at most `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.v_handover_ceiling_str`. At the chosen `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.v_handover_str`, the model predicts `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.f_handover_str`, inside the criterion.

The base's claim is a budget rather than a single force, and the delay components this chapter must evidence are the lease path and the observation age that its claims name. At the `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.v_aisle_str` aisle speed, the finished budget (@tbl-enforcement-stopping-budget) is `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.budget_str` against the `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.d_clear_str` clear distance, a spare of `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.spare_str`. That spare is the whole allowance for error in the budget's inputs. An unbudgeted delay of `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.t_spare_str`, the handover deadline $T_{\text{latest}}$ of @sec-intervention-authority-transitions, spends it, and so does a loaded deceleration `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.a_shortfall_pct_str` below the `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.a_brake_str` the budget assumes. A stopping claim whose inputs are unmeasured cannot show that its spare survives their errors.

The release question for the mobile manipulator has become three bounded criteria: the base stops inside the clear distance, the arm opens the door under the latch limit, and an item handover stays under the contact criterion. No calculation settles any of them alone, because each inherits premises about deceleration, delay, and contact that must themselves be evidenced, and each premise can lapse in service as brakes wear, floors soil, and sensors drift (@sec-release-standing-conditions). Connecting every claim to its premises, and every premise to its evidence, is the work of a safety case.

## Safety Cases and Claims {#sec-release-safety-cases-claims}

No inspection of the mobile manipulator can confirm that its loaded base will come to rest before it reaches a person at a rack end. That claim has to be decomposed until every branch ends in something measured, and a safety case is the structured argument that records the decomposition. Building on Stephen Toulmin's argument structure [@toulmin1958uses], Goal Structuring Notation (GSN)\index{Goal Structuring Notation}[^fn-std-gsn-argument] [@kelly1998arguing; @kelly2004goal], and the UL 4600 autonomy evaluation standard [@koopman2020how], this chapter constructs the claim-argument-evidence safety case of \ref{dfn-release-goal-structured-safety-case}\index{Claim-argument-evidence safety case!argument structure}. Its root is a claim that asserts a measurable physical property, such as the base's stop within the clear distance. Because that claim cannot be validated directly, strategies partition it by operating regime, hazard class, or subsystem, and each sub-claim ends in further sub-claims or in evidence, bounded by the context and assumptions under which its links hold.

[^fn-std-gsn-argument]: **Goal Structuring Notation**\index{Goal Structuring Notation!argumentation grammar}: Developed by Tim Kelly at the University of York, GSN provides an explicit graphical grammar for structuring and auditing safety assurance cases [@kelly1998arguing; @kelly2004goal]. The notation decomposes top-level safety goals into contextual sub-claims, argumentation strategies, and solutions grounded in test artifacts.

The structure's validity hinges on distinguishing evidence from demonstration. A **demonstration**\index{Demonstration!versus evidence} is a record of successful task execution over an uncharacterized test distribution, such as a long run of clean door openings with the strike plate always at its nominal position. It measures mean performance but bounds neither the tail nor the failure modes outside the sampled trajectory. Evidence is a falsifiable, calibrated artifact with quantified bounds, such as a worst-case timing distribution from hardware execution traces, loaded stopping trials across deceleration regimes, or a fault-injection trial that drives the machine to the boundary of its envelope. An artifact without quantified uncertainty, or one that never tests the boundary, remains a demonstration and cannot support an inferential link.

Connecting evidence to a claim requires a **warrant**\index{Warrant!inferential rule}, the inferential rule stating why the data support the assertion. For a learned policy the warrant is inductive, reasoning from failure-free test episodes to future service, and the exposure wall of @sec-evaluation-trial-limits shows why that link cannot carry a high-consequence claim alone. No zero-event campaign, on one machine or a fleet, reaches the hazard rates such claims name within any practical schedule. The argument must therefore add an architectural warrant, grounding the claim in an independent permission path (@sec-enforcement) that bounds actuator torque and withdraws motion whenever a learned command leaves the admitted set. That warrant narrows the claim rather than escaping the wall, since the permission path changes the claim only for the hazards it detects and stops in time (@sec-frontier-method-limits).

This tension between inductive fleet evidence and safety-critical assurance is illustrated by a decade of autonomous vehicle disengagement data reported to the California Department of Motor Vehicles (@fig-release-decade-california-dmv-disengagements). Between 2015 and 2025, developers logged tens of millions of public testing miles across California roads. Over this decade, Miles Between Disengagements (MPI) expanded across three distinct eras:

1. **Era I: Early Highway & Suburban Testing (2015–2018)**: Systems operated primarily on well-marked arterial corridors and highways. Developers established baseline autonomy cadences, scaling from hundreds of miles between human interventions to several thousand miles.
2. **Era II: Dense Urban Core Transition (2018–2021)**: Fleets migrated into dense metropolitan environments, most notably San Francisco's complex street grid. This environmental domain shift exposed uncharacterized edge cases—pedestrians stepping between double-parked vehicles, construction detour gestures, and dynamic occlusions—temporarily stalling or depressing reported MPI (e.g., Waymo's metric dropped from $29{,}945$ miles in 2020 to $7{,}965$ miles in 2021 before recovering).
3. **Era III: Commercial Driverless Scale & Divergence (2021–2025)**: Removal of the in-vehicle safety driver led to sharp strategic divergence. Waymo scaled rider-only commercial operations, exceeding $63{,}000$ miles per disengagement in 2025 across more than five million testing miles. Aurora pivoted its California passenger-car effort toward commercial Class 8 freight corridors in Texas. Apple cancelled its Project Titan initiative in early 2024 after a multi-billion-dollar R&D effort that struggled with early intervention sensitivity. Most instructively, Cruise crossed $80{,}000$ miles per disengagement in California filings shortly before an October 2023 pedestrian-dragging collision in San Francisco resulted in the immediate regulatory revocation of its autonomous testing and deployment permits.

The fundamental systems lesson of @fig-release-decade-california-dmv-disengagements is that an inductive warrant derived solely from aggregate fleet mileage cannot establish a catastrophic hazard claim. A high MPI indicates operational maturity under nominal conditions, but it does not bound the severity or probability of tail-event failures under unmodeled physical interactions. Safety cases for physical AI must combine empirical exposure with deterministic architectural enforcers that remain valid when learned policies encounter novel distributional shifts.

An engineering safety case does not exist in an institutional vacuum. Inside the development team, the claim-argument-evidence tree establishes technical confidence that physical risks are bounded; outside the team, it forms the evidential substrate for statutory regulatory authorization and legal accountability. When an autonomous system moves from the laboratory into commercial deployment, its safety claims intersect three primary governance pillars:

1. **The European Union AI Act (High-Risk Classification):** Under the EU Artificial Intelligence Act\index{EU AI Act!high-risk physical AI}\index{Regulatory compliance!EU AI Act}, AI systems deployed as safety components in physical machinery, collaborative robots, or autonomous transport are classified as *High-Risk AI Systems*. Statutory compliance mandates an auditable risk management system that spans the operational lifecycle, verified data governance documenting training and evaluation distributions (@sec-data-schema), human oversight interfaces capable of real-time intervention (@sec-intervention-human-authority), and tamper-evident event logging (@sec-intervention-trustworthy-logs) to ensure forensic reconstructibility after any anomalous contact.
2. **Domain-Specific Statutory Certification:** Beyond horizontal AI regulations, embodied systems must satisfy sector-specific safety mandates: the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA)\index{FDA!surgical robotics regulation} pre-market pathways (510(k) and De Novo) for autonomous surgical robotics, requiring human-factors validation under ANSI/AAMI HE75 and software lifecycle controls under IEC 62304; Federal Aviation Administration (FAA)\index{FAA!drone airworthiness} airworthiness certifications (Part 107/135) for autonomous aerial logistics; and UNECE/NHTSA standards (such as UN R157 for automated vehicle steering) governing automated driving systems.
3. **The Redistribution of Legal Liability:** In classical factory automation where robots operate within interlocked cages (@fig-industrial-welding), physical accidents are adjudicated primarily under the legal doctrine of *operator negligence*—evaluating whether floor personnel violated safety protocols or bypassed interlocks. When an autonomous machine operates without physical fencing in shared human spaces, legal responsibility shifts fundamentally toward *strict manufacturer product liability*\index{Product liability!strict liability in physical AI}\index{Legal liability!operator negligence versus strict liability}. An unmodeled perceptual failure or tracking overshoot is no longer an operator error; it is an alleged defect in design, manufacturing, or failure to instruct. In this legal regime, a cryptographically signed safety case and release manifest is not merely good engineering practice—it is the definitive evidentiary record establishing that the engineering team bounded residual risk to state-of-the-art standards prior to public release.

::: {#fig-release-decade-california-dmv-disengagements fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**A decade of autonomous vehicle disengagement trends reported to the California DMV (2015–2025)**: Annual Miles Between Disengagements (MPI, log scale) across major autonomous vehicle developers (Waymo, Cruise, Zoox, Apple Project Titan, and Aurora) spanning three historical operating eras. The horizontal dotted line marks the human driver baseline of approximately 40,000 miles between police-reported crashes (NHTSA). Milestones highlight Waymo's 2021 dense urban transition dip, Cruise's October 2023 permit revocation following a high-severity collision, Zoox's consistent urban robotaxi regime, Apple's program cancellation, and Waymo reaching 63,415 miles per disengagement in 2025.
```{python}
#| label: calc-release-low-light-age
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ AN UNSTATED LIGHTING ASSUMPTION IN THE STOPPING BUDGET
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-release-safety-cases-claims (contextual-assumptions paragraph).
# │ Goal: Show how a lighting change the budget never named ages the navigation
# │       camera's image, and what it would cost the aisle budget's spare
# │       if the age check did not refuse the frames.
# │ Show: nominal and low-light exposure, the added observation age, the added
# │       travel at aisle speed, and its share of the spare.
# │ How: perception age is timed from mid-exposure (AISLE.perception_age), so a
# │      longer exposure adds half its increase; spare from
# │      calc_safe_stopping_distance with a_eff, the constant deceleration
# │      whose distance matches calc_c2_stop_suffix.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, fmt_percent, check
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_safe_stopping_distance, calc_c2_effective_deceleration

# ┌── 1. LOAD: the running machine, plus one chapter-local input ────────────────
RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator  # category: illustrative (running machine)
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle  # category: illustrative (aisle scene; speeds, lease, and tick chosen)
low_light_exposure_factor = 2.0  # category: illustrative (scenario assumption: a dim aisle doubles the exposure)

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
t_exp_nominal = RM.nav_camera.exposure_time.to(millisecond)
t_exp_low = (low_light_exposure_factor * t_exp_nominal).to(millisecond)
dt_age = ((t_exp_low - t_exp_nominal) / 2).to(millisecond)  # mid-exposure timestamp
d_added = (AISLE.v_aisle * dt_age).to(millimeter)
a_eff = calc_c2_effective_deceleration(AISLE.a_brake)  # C2 stop suffix as an equivalent constant deceleration
budget = calc_safe_stopping_distance(AISLE.v_aisle, AISLE.tau_delay, a_eff, AISLE.delta_loc + AISLE.eps_track, AISLE.delta_margin).to(millimeter)
spare = (AISLE.d_clear - budget).to(millimeter)
share_of_spare = (d_added / spare).to("dimensionless").magnitude

# ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
check(abs(t_exp_nominal.magnitude - 16.0) < 1e-9, "Navigation-camera exposure 16 ms")
check(abs(dt_age.magnitude - 8.0) < 1e-9, "Low light adds 8 ms of observation age")
check(abs(d_added.magnitude - 10.4) < 1e-9, "10.4 mm of added travel at 1.3 m/s")
check(abs(spare.magnitude - 102.57) < 5e-3, "Spare at 1.3 m/s")
check(abs(share_of_spare - 0.101) < 5e-3, "About a tenth of the spare")

# ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
class ReleaseLowLight:
    t_exp_nominal_str = fmt_latency(t_exp_nominal, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_exp_low_str = fmt_latency(t_exp_low, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    dt_age_str = fmt_latency(dt_age, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    v_aisle_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_aisle, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    d_added_str = fmt_length(d_added, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    spare_str = fmt_length(round(spare.magnitude, 1) * millimeter, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    share_str = fmt_percent(round(share_of_spare * 100) / 100.0, precision=0, style="prose")
```

Every link also rests on contextual assumptions, and an unstated one is guarded only by whatever check happens to sit downstream of it. The stopping warrant assumes, among other conditions, that the aisle stays bright enough for the navigation camera's nominal exposure. Suppose a dim aisle doubles that exposure from `{python} ReleaseLowLight.t_exp_nominal_str` to `{python} ReleaseLowLight.t_exp_low_str`. Because an image's age is timed from mid-exposure, each observation arrives `{python} ReleaseLowLight.dt_age_str` older than the budget charges, which unchecked would carry the base another `{python} ReleaseLowLight.d_added_str` at the `{python} ReleaseLowLight.v_aisle_str` aisle speed, about `{python} ReleaseLowLight.share_str` of the budget's `{python} ReleaseLowLight.spare_str` spare. The permission path's age check refuses those frames instead, and the base stops in an aisle the case assumed it could run. The team meets its lighting assumption as unexplained lost service, and only a check that the case never tied to lighting kept it from becoming a silent loss of clearance. An assumption that no runtime check sees has no such backstop, as the localization allowance in the compound failure of @sec-release-adversarial-review shows. A sound argument therefore states every physical dependency as a bounded context element with a runtime monitor that detects its violation.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↳ **Downstream:** Epistemic assumptions embedded within safety case warrants are critically interrogated in @sec-frontier-epistemic-limits.
:::

The weakest link governs every claim-argument-evidence tree. A safety case is not an aggregate in which over-performance in one branch compensates for a deficit in another. High accuracy on a recognition benchmark does not offset an uncharacterized latency tail on the CAN bus, nor does extensive policy simulation offset missing brake-wear data. If the base's stop decomposes into sub-claims for braking, thermal protection of the drives (@sec-body-thermal-duty-cycles), and trajectory bounding, a failed warrant in any one branch invalidates the root claim. The reviewer who adjudicates the case therefore looks not for the number of supporting artifacts but for the single weakest link whose failure would permit harm.

### Match the safety argument to the machine

```{python}
#| label: calc-release-claims
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE SIX RELEASE CLAIMS ON THE RUNNING MACHINE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-release-safety-cases-claims (scorecard lead-in) and
# │          @tbl-16-cae-scorecard.
# │ Goal: Instance claims C1-C6 on the warehouse mobile manipulator.
# │ Show: base budget at aisle speed against the clear distance; latch force at
# │       brake command, remaining compression, and the arm stop it requires;
# │       mug pick and handover speeds with the handover ceiling and force;
# │       renewal-to-onset time; enforcer WCET and deadline; friction needed
# │       for a_brake; observation age; the handover deadline T_latest at the
# │       in-loop takeover slow-down and at aisle speed.
# │ How: RM/AISLE fields; calc_safe_stopping_distance with the calc_c2_stop_suffix
# │      distance as an equivalent constant deceleration;
# │      calc_tripwire_contact_force_accumulation; calc_transient_impact_force.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_force, fmt_mass, fmt_latency, fmt_acceleration, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, check
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import (
    calc_safe_stopping_distance,
    calc_c2_effective_deceleration,
    calc_latch_contact_stopping_profile,
    calc_transient_impact_force,
)

# ┌── 1. LOAD: the running machine and its site ─────────────────────────────────
RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator  # category: illustrative (running machine)
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle  # category: illustrative (aisle scene; speeds, lease, and tick chosen)
g_std = (1 * ureg.standard_gravity).to(meter / second**2)  # category: datasheet (standard gravity, a defined physical constant; Pint)

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE: one warrant quantity per claim ────────────────────────────────
# C1 base: finished budget at aisle speed.
a_eff = calc_c2_effective_deceleration(AISLE.a_brake)  # C2 stop suffix as an equivalent constant deceleration
budget_aisle = calc_safe_stopping_distance(AISLE.v_aisle, AISLE.tau_delay, a_eff, AISLE.delta_loc + AISLE.eps_track, AISLE.delta_margin).to(
    millimeter
)
spare_aisle = (AISLE.d_clear - budget_aisle).to(millimeter)
# C1 door: force at brake command and the arm stop that keeps it under the limit.
latch_stop = calc_latch_contact_stopping_profile(scenario=AISLE)
f_cmd = latch_stop["f_at_brake_onset"]
x_remaining = latch_stop["x_remaining"]
a_arm_needed = latch_stop["a_arm_needed"]
# C1 handover: unbraked elastic force at the handover speed.
f_handover = calc_transient_impact_force(AISLE.v_handover, RM.arm_effective_contact_mass, AISLE.k_contact_human).to(newton)
# C2: last valid renewal to brake onset.
t_renewal_to_onset = (AISLE.t_lease + AISLE.t_tick + AISLE.t_bus + AISLE.t_brake_onset).to(millisecond)
# C3: friction the credible deceleration needs.
mu_min = (AISLE.a_brake / g_std).to("dimensionless").magnitude
v_handover_ceiling = (AISLE.f_contact_criterion / (AISLE.k_contact_human * RM.arm_effective_contact_mass) ** 0.5).to(meter / second)
# C6: an unacknowledged handover falls back by the spare spent as time, at the
# in-loop takeover slow-down (operative) and at aisle speed (a policy request).
t_timeout = (spare_aisle / AISLE.v_aisle).to(millisecond)
budget_takeover = calc_safe_stopping_distance(
    AISLE.v_takeover_in_loop, AISLE.tau_delay, a_eff, AISLE.delta_loc + AISLE.eps_track, AISLE.delta_margin
).to(millimeter)
spare_takeover = (AISLE.d_clear - budget_takeover).to(millimeter)
t_latest_takeover = (spare_takeover / AISLE.v_takeover_in_loop).to(millisecond)

# ┌── 3. GUARD: canon values quoted in the table ────────────────────────────────
check(abs(budget_aisle.magnitude - 997.43) < 5e-3, "C1 base budget at 1.3 m/s")
check(budget_aisle < AISLE.d_clear, "C1 budget fits inside the clear distance")
check(abs(f_cmd.magnitude - 39.0) < 1e-9, "C1 latch force at brake command")
check(abs(x_remaining.magnitude - 0.1525) < 1e-6, "C1 remaining compression 0.15 mm")
check(abs(a_arm_needed.magnitude - 2.95) < 0.005, "C1 arm stop premise about 3 m/s^2 (computed 2.95)")
check(abs(f_handover.magnitude - 42.43) < 0.01, "C1 handover force 42.4 N")
check(f_handover < AISLE.f_contact_criterion, "C1 handover force under the criterion")
check(abs(t_renewal_to_onset.magnitude - 82.0) < 1e-9, "C2 renewal-to-onset 82 ms")
check(AISLE.enforcer_wcet < AISLE.enforcer_deadline < AISLE.t_tick, "C2 WCET < deadline < tick")
check(abs(mu_min - 0.204) < 5e-4, "C3 friction floor 0.204")
check(abs(AISLE.perception_age.to(millisecond).magnitude - 51.6) < 1e-9, "C4 age 51.6 ms")
check(abs(t_timeout.magnitude - 78.9) < 0.05, "C6 fallback by 78.9 ms at 1.3 m/s")
check(abs(spare_takeover.magnitude - 209.7) < 0.05, "C6 spare 209.7 mm at the 1.2 m/s slow-down")
check(abs(t_latest_takeover.magnitude - 174.7) < 0.05, "C6 fallback by 174.7 ms at 1.2 m/s")
check(abs(RM.tcp_speed_limit.to(meter / second).magnitude - 1.0) < 1e-9, "C1 mug pick under the 1.0 m/s TCP limit")
check(abs(v_handover_ceiling.magnitude - 0.1179) < 5e-5, "C1 handover ceiling 0.118 m/s")

# ┌── 4. OUTPUT: rendered values ────────────────────────────────────────────────
class ReleaseClaims:
    budget_str = fmt_length(round(budget_aisle.magnitude, 1) * millimeter, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    v_aisle_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_aisle, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(AISLE.d_clear, unit=meter, precision=2)
    f_cmd_str = fmt_force(f_cmd, precision=0)
    x_remaining_str = fmt_length(round(x_remaining.magnitude, 2) * millimeter, unit=millimeter, precision=2)
    a_arm_str = fmt_acceleration(round(a_arm_needed.magnitude) * meter / second**2, unit=meter / second**2, precision=0)
    f_latch_limit_str = fmt_force(AISLE.f_latch_limit, precision=0)
    f_handover_str = fmt_force(f_handover, precision=1)
    v_handover_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_handover, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    f_contact_str = fmt_force(AISLE.f_contact_criterion, precision=0)
    m1_str = fmt_mass(RM.loaded_mass, unit=kilogram, precision=0)
    t_renewal_to_onset_str = fmt_latency(t_renewal_to_onset, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    wcet_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.enforcer_wcet, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    deadline_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.enforcer_deadline, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    mu_min_str = fmt(round(mu_min, 3), precision=3)
    t_age_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.perception_age, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_timeout_str = fmt_latency(round(t_timeout.magnitude, 1) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_latest_takeover_str = fmt_latency(round(t_latest_takeover.magnitude, 1) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    v_takeover_in_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_takeover_in_loop, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    v_tcp_str = fmt_velocity(RM.tcp_speed_limit, unit=meter / second, precision=0)
    v_handover_ceiling_str = fmt_velocity(round(v_handover_ceiling.magnitude, 3) * meter / second, unit=meter / second, precision=3)
```

For the mobile manipulator's arm, ISO 10218-1 and ISO 10218-2 frame the robot and integration assessment, and ISO/TS 15066 informs the collaborative-contact case once the argument names the contacted body region, pressure, geometry, and measurement method [@isots15066]. The base's claims, which make up most of the case, are argued from its measured stopping budget and the site survey. The road-vehicle standards ISO 26262\index{Functional safety!ISO 26262} and ISO 21448\index{ISO 21448!SOTIF} lend the argument their distinction between faults and limits of intended function but certify nothing about this machine [@iso26262; @iso21448].

The claim-argument-evidence scorecard in @tbl-16-cae-scorecard states six claims and pairs each physical warrant with its adjudication on this book's evidence. Claim C3 shows the decision: an oil film can defeat braking traction, so nominal model accuracy cannot justify an unrestricted verdict. A physically realizable condition that invalidates a warrant in this way is its **defeater**\index{Defeaters!definition}, and @sec-release-adversarial-review turns the search for defeaters into a review method. Claim C6 stands only on the fault records that test the four authority rules @sec-intervention-authority-log hands over (A1–A4).

|:----------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| C1. Contact and stopping    | Base: stop of `{python} ReleaseClaims.budget_str` at `{python} ReleaseClaims.v_aisle_str` (@tbl-enforcement-stopping-budget) inside the `{python} ReleaseClaims.d_clear_str` clear distance to a person standing at the rack end, with the payload untested at `{python} ReleaseClaims.m1_str` an open premise; Door: latch force of `{python} ReleaseClaims.f_cmd_str` at brake command, with the arm stopping within a further `{python} ReleaseClaims.x_remaining_str` (about `{python} ReleaseClaims.a_arm_str`) under the `{python} ReleaseClaims.f_latch_limit_str` limit; Mug: picked from the conveyor under the `{python} ReleaseClaims.v_tcp_str` TCP limit on tracked intent and handed to the coworker at `{python} ReleaseClaims.v_handover_str`, under the derived `{python} ReleaseClaims.v_handover_ceiling_str` ceiling, with a contact force of `{python} ReleaseClaims.f_handover_str` under the `{python} ReleaseClaims.f_contact_str` criterion, and the grasped object taken to be the mug the task names | `REFUSE`: credible deceleration, brake onset, tracking and localization error, arm deceleration, and tissue stiffness are illustrative; the grounding premise is unknown |
